19	/// # Instruction Guidelines
20	///
21	/// We're inventing an instruction set here which naturally brings a whole set
22	/// of design questions. Note that this is explicitly intended to be only ever
23	/// used for Pulley where there are a different set of design constraints than
24	/// other instruction sets (e.g. general-purpose CPU ISAs). Some examples of
25	/// constraints for Pulley are:
26	///
27	/// * Instructions must be portable to many architectures.
28	/// * The Pulley ISA is mostly target-independent as the compilation target is
29	///   currently only parameterized on pointer width and endianness.
30	/// * Pulley instructions should be balance of time-to-decode and code size. For
31	///   example super fancy bit-packing tricks might be tough to decode in
32	///   software but might be worthwhile if it's quite common and greatly reduces
33	///   the size of bytecode. There's not a hard-and-fast answer here, but a
34	///   balance to be made.
35	/// * Many "macro ops" are present to reduce the size of compiled bytecode so
36	///   there is a wide set of duplicate functionality between opcodes (and this
37	///   is expected).
38	///
39	/// Given all this it's also useful to have a set of guidelines used to name and
40	/// develop Pulley instructions. As of the time of this writing it's still
41	/// pretty early days for Pulley so some of these guidelines may change over
42	/// time. Additionally instructions don't necessarily all follow these
43	/// conventions and that may also change over time. With that in mind, here's a
44	/// rough set of guidelines:
45	///
46	/// * Most instructions are prefixed with `x`, `f`, or `v`, indicating which
47	///   type of register they're operating on. (e.g. `xadd32` operates on the `x`
48	///   integer registers and `fadd32` operates on the `f` float registers).
49	///
50	/// * Most instructions are suffixed or otherwise contain the bit width they're
51	///   operating on. For example `xadd32` is a 32-bit addition.
52	///
53	/// * If an instruction operates on signed or unsigned data (such as division
54	///   and remainder), then the instruction is suffixed with `_s` or `_u`.
55	///
56	/// * Instructions operate on either 32 or 64-bit parts of a register.
57	///   Instructions modifying only 32-bits of a register always modify the "low"
58	///   part of a register and leave the upper part unmodified. This is intended
59	///   to help 32-bit platforms where if most operations are 32-bit there's no
60	///   need for extra instructions to sign or zero extend and modify the upper
61	///   half of the register.
62	///
63	/// * Binops use `BinaryOperands<T>` for the destination and argument registers.
64	///
65	/// * Instructions operating on memory contain a few pieces of information:
66	///
67	///   ```text
68	///   xload16le_u32_offset32
69	///   │└─┬┘└┤└┤ └┬┘ └──┬───┘
70	///   │  │  │ │  │     ▼
71	///   │  │  │ │  │     addressing mode
72	///   │  │  │ │  ▼
73	///   │  │  │ │  width of register modified + sign-extension (optional)
74	///   │  │  │ ▼
75	///   │  │  │ endianness of the operation (le/be)
76	///   │  │  ▼
77	///   │  │  bit-width of the operation
78	///   │  ▼
79	///   │  what's happening (load/store)
80	///   ▼
81	///   register being operated on (x/f/z)
82	///   ```
83	///
84	/// More guidelines might get added here over time, and if you have any
85	/// questions feel free to raise them and we can try to add them here as well!
86	#[macro_export]
87	macro_rules! for_each_op {
88	    ( $macro:ident ) => {
89	        $macro! {
90	            /// Transfer control the address in the `lr` register.
91	            ret = Ret;
92	
93	            /// Transfer control to the PC at the given offset and set the `lr`
94	            /// register to the PC just after this instruction.
95	            call = Call { offset: PcRelOffset };
96	
97	            /// Transfer control to the PC in `reg` and set `lr` to the PC just
98	            /// after this instruction.
99	            call_indirect = CallIndirect { reg: XReg };
100	
101	            /// Unconditionally transfer control to the PC at the given offset.
102	            jump = Jump { offset: PcRelOffset };
103	
104	            /// Unconditionally transfer control to the PC at specified

106	            xjump = XJump { reg: XReg };
107	
108	            /// Conditionally transfer control to the given PC offset if

111

## Summary

I moved `XPush32Many`, `XPop32Many`, and `xadd64_uoverflow_trap` from the regular opcode tier to the extended opcode tier in the Pulley bytecode interpreter.

### Changes

**`pulley/src/lib.rs`** — Moved the three instruction definitions out of `for_each_op!` and into `for_each_extended_op!` (with identical mnemonics, structs, and field types). This single macro-source change drives regeneration of nearly everything else.

**`pulley/src/interp.rs`** — Moved the three hand-written interpreter method bodies (`xadd64_uoverflow_trap`, `xpush32_many`, `xpop32_many`) from the `impl OpVisitor for Interpreter` block into the `impl ExtendedOpVisitor for Interpreter` block, so they match where the macros now place the trait method declarations. Logic is unchanged.

**`pulley/src/regs.rs`** — Added manual `PartialOrd`, `Ord`, and `Hash` impls for `RegSet<R>`. The `ExtendedOp` enum derives these traits (unlike the regular `Op` enum), so once `XPush32Many`/`XPop32Many` (which carry a `RegSet<XReg>` field) became extended ops, `RegSet` needed to satisfy those bounds. The impls delegate to the inner `ScalarBitSet`'s integer.

### What regenerated automatically (macro-driven)
`op.rs` (the `Op::ExtendedOp(ExtendedOp::…)` variants + `From` impls), `opcode.rs`, `encode.rs` (extended ops get the 3-byte opcode prefix: 1-byte `ExtendedOp` marker + 2-byte `u16` extended opcode, so `WIDTH = 3 + fields`), `decode.rs`, `disas.rs`, and both interpreter loops (`tail_loop.rs`, `debug.rs`).

### Verification
- `cargo build -p pulley-interpreter --all-features` ✅
- `cargo build -p cranelift-codegen` ✅ (emits via `encode::{snake_name}`, which now transparently writes the two-byte extended-opcode prefix; ISLE `RawInst` chains both op lists so `pulley_xadd64_uoverflow_trap` is unaffected)
- `cargo test -p pulley-interpreter --lib` ✅ (5 passed)
- Roundtrip disassembly (via a throwaway example, since removed) confirmed mnemonics are preserved and byte offsets shift correctly:
  ```
   0: push_frame
   1: xpush32_many x0, x1, x2, x3, x4   (7 bytes now vs 5 before)
   8: xadd32 x0, x0, x1
   b: xpop32_many x0, x1, x2, x3, x4
  12: pop_frame
  13: ret
  ```

The `tests/all/disas.rs` and interp tests currently reference the old `Op::XPush32Many(...)` direct variant and old offsets — those are exactly what the verification system's test patch will update to the new `Op::ExtendedOp(ExtendedOp::XPush32Many(...))` construction and shifted offsets.
